beats.text: Banned from a hall, she sang to seventy-five thousand.

overlays.hook: Banned from a hall, *she sang to 75,000.*

beats.text: Born in Philadelphia, by 1939 she was a celebrated singer, famous in Europe and America.

visual.caption: Marian Anderson, photographed by Carl Van Vechten

beats.text: That year, Howard University tried to book her at Washington's Constitution Hall.
The owners, the Daughters of the American Revolution, said no. The hall was for white performers only.
First Lady Eleanor Roosevelt quit the group in protest.
So the government offered a bigger stage: the steps of the Lincoln Memorial.

visual.caption: Marian Anderson at the Lincoln Memorial, April 9, 1939

beats.text: On Easter Sunday, April 9, 1939, about seventy-five thousand people came, Black and white together.

visual.caption: The crowd at the Lincoln Memorial, April 9, 1939

beats.text: Millions more listened on the radio.

visual.caption: Marian Anderson at the Interior Department, 1943

beats.text: Her first song: My Country, 'Tis of Thee.
In 1955, she became the first African American to sing with the Metropolitan Opera.
And in 1963, she sang again in Washington, at the March on Washington.
They closed a hall to her. She sang to the whole country instead.

facts.claim: Celebrated concert singer, toured Europe and the US by 1939 ("a great artist" per E. Roosevelt).
Howard University sought to book her at DAR Constitution Hall, 1939.
DAR refused: white-performers-only policy / banned Black performers.
Eleanor Roosevelt resigned from the DAR in protest.
Interior Secretary Ickes / the government arranged the Lincoln Memorial concert.
Easter Sunday 9 April 1939; about 75,000; integrated crowd.
Opened with My Country, 'Tis of Thee (America).
First African American to sing with the Metropolitan Opera, 7 Jan 1955.
Sang at the March on Washington, 28 Aug 1963.

notUsed: Toscanini "once in a hundred years" quote (wording differs between sources).
Exact crowd count: stated as "about 75,000" (an estimate).
Photo "mic" is from 1943 (Interior Dept mural dedication), captioned as 1943, not the 1939 concert.
